slides.headline: October 5, 1864: a cyclone killed 60,000 people in Calcutta - and accidentally built India's weather-warning system.
A storm surge roughly 40 feet high tore up the Hooghly River and devastated Calcutta
slides.body: The Great Calcutta Cyclone of October 5, 1864, wrecked hundreds of ships, flattened warehouses across the port, and killed an estimated 60,000 people - one of the deadliest cyclones ever recorded. There had been no warning system of any kind.

slides.headline: The catastrophe forced British India to start taking weather seriously - as an institution, not an afterthought.
slides.body: The scale of the disaster exposed how unprepared the region was, and became one of the direct pressures that led to organized meteorological observation in India - culminating in the founding of the India Meteorological Department on January 15, 1875.

slides.eyebrow: Why it matters for Viksit Bharat 2047
slides.headline: India's disaster-preparedness institutions trace back to a tragedy nobody saw coming.
slides.body: A Viksit Bharat by 2047 depends on the kind of forecasting and warning infrastructure that didn't exist in 1864 - built precisely because that absence once cost tens of thousands of lives.

sources.text: The Tribune - The Calcutta Cyclone of 1864: From catastrophe to India's cyclone-warning system
